claims.title: Abstract empirical totals and guarded negative interpretation
claims.paper_text: A lost submission response can leave a generation client uncertain whether its backend executed a request. We describe an evidence exporter, a same-run submission guard, and controlled fault injection for local image-generation pipelines. The exporter separates reported state, interpretation, and oracle evidence. Four fixed Windows/ComfyUI cases retained one execution binding per control and two per response-loss case; their second calls created fresh runs outside the guard. A subsequent two-case same-run campaign retained raw transport, but model-identity validation rejected its retry before the ambiguity guard. Zero additional submissions therefore do not establish that guard's efficacy. Synthetic CPU fixtures exercise its blocking behavior and expose incomplete operation as a cost. Raw payloads support reconstruction of the new retained bindings, while the historical event gap remains. Original-run reconciliation, deployment rates, physical GPU execution counts and output-quality improvements remain unestablished.
claims.paper_value: Abstract empirical totals and guarded negative interpretation
claims.evidence_value: Historical controls 1 binding each; historical response-loss cases 2 each; new campaign 2 cases; no added F02 submission; target guard not observed.
claims.details: Repeated detailed claims are audited individually below. This is retained evidence consistency, not authentication.

claims.title: Implementation comprises export, run guard and separate observation boundaries
claims.paper_text:
Our prototype combines persistent run records, generation orchestration,
a ComfyUI adapter and artifact handling. We describe tooling that preserves the
client's evidence, applies versioned interpretation rules, and records backend
observations independently of the client's returned status. Its product guard
is deliberately narrower: an explicitly unknown submission blocks further
submission through the same unresolved run at the reviewed entry points.

The tool description has three parts: an evidence representation and read-only
exporter; a same-run guard whose unresolved state remains visible; and CPU and
Windows fault-observation workflows with separate evidence boundaries. The
Windows demonstration tests visibility across the client--backend boundary.
It does not establish that the guard reduces execution counts in that protocol.
The contribution is an inspectable integration of evidence interpretation,
run-scoped control and backend observation. Section~\ref{sec:related} compares its scope with
idempotent APIs, workflow execution and tracing. The evaluated contribution
is this implementation and its failure windows.

claims.evidence_value: Implementation source is not in the declared input set.
claims.details: Recorded results do not establish every entry-point implementation property.
claims.fix: Supply source inspection inputs if implementation verification is required.

claims.title: Product calls, submissions and execution observations are distinct; F00/F02/F03 scope
claims.paper_text:
A \textbf{product call} is an invocation by the research client. A \textbf{run} is the
persistent product object created by \texttt{local\_gpu\_start\_run}. A \textbf{submission} in
the Windows results is a proxy-observed \texttt{POST /prompt}; a call that fails before
that boundary need not produce a submission. An \textbf{execution instance} is an
observation bound to backend execution events. CPU fixtures instead observe
the synthetic worker entry. These units are not interchangeable.

F00 is a normal control. F02 suppresses the first accepted submission response,
creating a window in which the client lacks an acknowledged job identifier.
F03, covered by the CPU fixtures rather than the Windows campaign reported
here, concerns loss of completion information after a job identifier is known.
An explicit rejection and a missing response have different evidential meanings.
Neither should be silently converted into a backend execution outcome.
claims.paper_value: Product calls, submissions and execution observations are distinct; F00/F02/F03 scope
claims.evidence_value: Same-run F02 has 2 calls, 1 POST and 1 retained lifecycle; CPU matrix has F00/F02/F03, Windows records have F00/F02.
claims.details: Operational units and scope match the retained records.

claims.title: Research-client resolved/unresolved labels and durable-state distinction
claims.paper_text:
The evidence model distinguishes reported state, interpreted state and oracle
state. In addition, the Windows research client emits its own call-level labels.
Its \texttt{resolved} label is derived from a generated product result after checking
for artifact hashes. Its \texttt{unresolved} label can arise from several client errors.
Thus a research-client label alone does not prove that a durable product
manifest has a particular recovery state. In F02, the proxy's accepted-response
loss and the oracle binding provide the additional context.

claims.title: Versioned exporter policy, provenance limits and exclusive non-mutating output
claims.paper_text:
The exporter accepts a record or run manifest and produces a separate normalized
record. It copies reported state, records the mapping version and reasons, and
retains supplied oracle state separately. The schema includes source identity,
request and input digests, backend identity, job identifier, artifact hash and
validator version. Missing fields carry explicit reasons instead of fabricated
values. The inspected mapping is \texttt{research-normalization-v3}.

Interpretation checks more than an execution-success label. Job and artifact
bindings, approval and validation evidence, and recovery state constrain the
\texttt{execution\_verified} decision. An unresolved recovery state prevents this flag
from becoming true even when other evidence reports successful execution.
The current mapping also keeps recovery unknown when the reported run state is
missing and marks a disagreement between manifest and selected job or artifact
identity as an evidence mismatch. These rules prevent omission or a top-level
field from silently strengthening the composite decision.
This permits the record to express backend completion without asserting that
the product's recovery obligation has been discharged. The exporter does not
invoke the engine, retry a request or update the source run. Its output writer
uses exclusive file creation. These are implementation properties, not a
claim of complete filesystem security.
The interpretation assumes that supplied oracle and artifact-validator records
have trustworthy provenance. The exporter checks their stated fields and
bindings; it does not authenticate their origin or reconstruct missing raw
events. In the current mapping, absent source revision, backend-instance or
validator-version metadata need not by themselves prevent
\texttt{execution\_verified}. That flag denotes satisfaction of this mapping's
evidence policy, not independent certification of the input record.
claims.paper_value: Versioned exporter policy, provenance limits and exclusive non-mutating output
claims.evidence_value: No exporter source or normalized outputs were declared.
claims.details: The declared raw records cannot validate research-normalization-v3, exclusive creation, unknown-state policy or metadata veto rules.
claims.fix: Include exporter source and mapping fixtures in an implementation audit.

claims.title: Read-only exporter command and separate observer/normalizer interfaces
claims.paper_text:
An investigator first inspects the run manifest and the recorded submission
outcome. If submission is explicitly unknown, inspection must preserve that
uncertainty: the missing job identifier must not be synthesized from a later
successful call. Backend observation is then associated with the relevant
request and execution instance, while artifact checks retain their own result.
The export command writes a new record and refuses to overwrite an existing
export:
\begin{quote}\small\ttfamily
python -m\\
scripts.research.export\_records\\
--input run-record.json --output evidence.json
\end{quote}
The exported record lets a reader inspect reported state, interpreted state,
mapping reasons and oracle evidence without invoking recovery. It does not
acquire a missing oracle automatically. The Windows observer export and the
normalized exporter schema are separate interfaces; a complete automatic
conversion between them is not established by the pilot.

claims.evidence_value: No command output or exporter code in the declared set.

claims.title: Unresolved backend completion can coexist with blocked same-run recovery; no automatic reconciliation
claims.paper_text:
For example, an unresolved run and successful backend evidence may coexist.
The execution field can describe the observed backend outcome while recovery
remains required and execution verification remains false. This separation is
the intended diagnostic output, rather than an error to hide by replacing the
original run state with the latest call's result.

\subsection{Recovery guard and its scope}

\texttt{AssetRunEngine} and \texttt{RunStore} preserve the explicit transport marker
\texttt{submission\_outcome=unknown} as an unresolved attempt. The reviewed submission
entry checks that unresolved attempt before permitting further generation.
The guard applies within the same run, including attempts with a different
idempotency key. The corresponding inspection action is \texttt{get\_run}.

This guard does not discover a missing backend job identifier or reconcile an
unknown job automatically. A newly created run lies outside the prior run's
guard. Existing recovery for a known job in a two-stage operation is a separate
path and is not attributed to this no-job-ID guard. The resulting tradeoff is
explicit: the guard withholds another submission through that run while the
required evidence is unavailable; it does not guarantee eventual completion.

claims.evidence_value: W3 F02 cases retain completed synthetic lifecycles, unresolved product state and outcome_unknown_blocked.
claims.details: Observed fixture behavior supports this bounded claim; different-key entry-point universality requires source evidence.

claims.title: Potential pre-acceptance false positive separated from observed accepted-response-loss completion cost
claims.paper_text:
A pipeline integrator can use this distinction when a generation UI receives a
disconnect after sending a request: the exporter preserves the unknown outcome,
the same-run entry blocks another submission, and the operator must inspect or
reconcile the run through an available backend-specific mechanism. The guard can
also conservatively withhold work when a request failed before backend acceptance,
which is a potential false-positive direction. In the accepted-response-loss
CPU fixture, the observed cost is an incomplete client operation; eventual
completion is not established.

claims.title: Shim endpoint preservation, observer connection ordering and identifier construction
claims.paper_text:
Figure~\ref{fig:architecture} shows the product and research boundaries.
The research harness adds a transport shim and loopback fault proxy. The shim
routes prompt transport through the proxy while retaining the actual backend
endpoint in the product's identity client. F02 drops the first response only
after backend acceptance. This arrangement is a research instrument, not a
native ComfyUI recovery feature.

The observer connects before the product invocation and uses the operation key
as its ComfyUI client identifier, matching the product's event-routing identity.
\texttt{ComfyUIEventOracle} requires an execution-start event, a terminal event and
completed history bound to a prompt identifier. It derives an execution-instance
identifier using the backend boot identity, prompt identifier and observed
start sequence. Its independence is from the product return value: it still
trusts the backend's event and history interfaces, and it is not a physical GPU
monitor or a crash-durable audit log.

claims.title: Historical second calls create fresh runs, use seed 4100 + call_index, and digest excludes seed/plan
claims.paper_text:
The controller permits the second F02 product call only after the first
execution has a bindable completion. In this historical protocol, the client creates a new run on each call
and uses \texttt{seed = 4100 + call\_index}. This is observation-gated fresh-run
generation, not automatic reconciliation of the original run. Because the new
run is outside the same-run guard, the Windows campaign does not measure the
guard's blocking effect. CPU F02 fixtures exercise blocking; in the single-stage
fixture, W3 has one execution rather than B2's two, while leaving the operation incomplete. Matching frozen
request digests does not establish full prompt equality: the inspected digest
function excludes the seed and does not use its plan argument.

claims.title: Related-work contracts and documentation-based scope comparison
claims.paper_text:
RPC failure semantics provide the conceptual starting point: a failed
communication does not necessarily settle whether a remote operation ran \cite{birrell1984}.
Idempotent API design addresses safe retries through an explicit contract,
including caller-provided request identifiers \cite{aws}. Our tool relies on neither
a prompt identifier nor a client idempotency key as sufficient evidence of
backend deduplication. Its role is to preserve and qualify observations when
such a guarantee has not been established for the evaluated path.

The practical distinction is between observation and control. Backend events
can establish that work completed while the client's original run remains
unresolved. Conversely, a conservative same-run guard can block a further
submission without resolving that uncertainty. The Windows harness crosses a
different boundary by creating a new run after observation. Keeping these
scopes separate explains why the demonstration can be oracle-evaluable without
showing automatic recovery or a W3 reduction in executions.

A recent preprint by Li studies ambiguous writes in a simulated service
benchmark, comparing model, harness and tool-contract effects on duplicate
side effects \cite{li2026exactlyonce}. Its guard combines read-back verification,
idempotency keys where supported, delayed re-verification, blocking unverifiable
non-idempotent repeats, and uncertainty annotations. Our guard has a narrower
control rule: an explicitly unknown submission blocks further submission through
the same run, without automatic read-back or reconciliation. The shared principle
of withholding unsafe retries is not a novelty claim. The tool-specific object
here is the inspectable integration of preserved reported state, versioned
interpretation with reasons, and backend observation in a local generation
pipeline. This is an implementation distinction, not evidence of superiority
over that guard or of a new general recovery principle. The studies use different
workloads and evidence sources; their outcome counts are not directly comparable.

Reliable State Machines provide a stronger control contract within their
programming model: persistent state and runtime-managed atomic processing
support failure transparency and exactly-once input processing
\cite{rsm2019}. Our tool does not place the external generator inside such a
transactional runtime. It exposes uncertainty at that boundary and restricts
one product entry path, rather than claiming an equivalent processing guarantee.

Temporal's Activity documentation describes the same lost-completion boundary:
a worker may finish an Activity and crash before reporting completion, leading
to a retry. It recommends idempotent Activities \cite{temporal}. This is an important
comparison because durable workflow state alone does not eliminate uncertainty
about external side effects. Our same-run guard withholds a submission under
explicit uncertainty, but supplies no equivalent general workflow-execution or
automatic reconciliation guarantee.

OpenTelemetry represents operations through spans and uses trace context to
relate observations across a request \cite{otel}. Such correlation provides a useful
representation for a distributed execution path. In this tool, the additional
application-specific rule is which observations permit an execution claim:
backend start and terminal events must bind to completed history, and unresolved
product recovery can still veto \texttt{execution\_verified}. Correlation identifiers
alone are not used as execution counts.

Toxiproxy provides configurable TCP connection fault injection for testing \cite{toxiproxy}.
Our research proxy uses an application-level acceptance condition to select
the response to suppress, while the observer separately checks execution. This
comparison does not show that Toxiproxy could not support an equivalent setup;
no comparative implementation or usability measurement was performed.

Filibuster's project overview describes synthesizing fault-injected test
variations from developer integration tests to check application error handling
\cite{filibuster}. Our fixed case set does not provide that automatic search
coverage. It concentrates on evidence interpretation at a selected submission
barrier and preserves a separate backend observation channel. The comparison
uses the project overview, not a reproduction of Filibuster's research results.

This is a documentation-based comparison of responsibilities, not a performance
benchmark or a feature-absence survey. The practical contribution is making the
relationship between client ambiguity, backend observation and permitted claims
inspectable for a local generation workflow. The comparisons delimit the tool
responsibilities; they do not establish superiority, exhaustive novelty,
or measured developer productivity.

claims.title: Conclusion distinguishes historical visibility, masked same-run guard and unsupported general guarantees
claims.paper_text:
The tool preserves ambiguous client outcomes alongside separately bound
execution evidence and implements a conservative guard within an unresolved
run. The historical Windows cases demonstrate execution visibility under lost
acceptance responses, while exposing the distinction between a new successful
call and reconciliation of the original run. These bounded observations support
an evidence-preserving tool description. The same-run test adds raw-event
retention and a negative result: model-identity validation masks the target
guard. It establishes neither guard efficacy nor new physical GPU work.
These results do not establish automatic
unknown-job recovery, deployment-wide reliability or natural duplicate-execution
rates.

claims.title: Package redistribution, human-subject and AI-usage statements
claims.paper_text:
\section*{Data, code and responsible use}
The manuscript source includes derived Windows evidence, retained CPU-record
pointers, a deterministic audit script and figure sources. Models, private
configuration, generated images and raw host paths are not redistributed in
this package. The analysis concerns controlled software executions; it makes
no claim about human participants or image-quality acceptance. Human-subjects
or institutional-ethics determinations are not inferred from this scope.

\section*{AI Tool Usage}
OpenAI Codex assisted with drafting portions of the manuscript, source
inspection, record consistency checks, and code for Figs.~1--2. The review
conducted with this tool was internal and within a single context, not
independent peer review. Human authors must verify the content, references,
attribution, and final submission. No AI-generated data are reported as
experimental observations.
